paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with spatial, embodied, physical, and temporal reasoning. We hypothesize that these failures reflect a shared deficit in visual transition reasoning, and test whether this capability can serve as a shared training primitive, one that different models can learn from different supervision sources and reuse across different tasks, with a systematic training recipe. Existing benchmarks document these deficits separately but do not support controlled comparisons across scenes, actions, and reasoning operations. We therefore introduce WOVEN, a training source and benchmark for visual transition reasoning that organizes transition supervision by scene, action, and reasoning type, using diverse, realistic rollouts from video-pretrained generative models: 36,076 examples across 20 scene types, 5 action types, and 8 reasoning types. We first evaluate 38 frontier MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B) and find a substantial and systematic deficit: even the strongest models fall far below humans, and the failures recur across model families and persist with scale. We then train MLLMs at multiple scales on WOVEN and find that they learn a shared capability that transfers broadly: training subsets of only about 2,000 items each collectively improve 22 of 26 external benchmarks by up to 27.3 percentage points, and WOVEN data can replace 30-50% of a task's own training data with comparable accuracy. Controlled comparisons further yield a training recipe for visual world modeling, validated prospectively on held-out benchmarks: select supervision by the reasoning operation it teaches rather than by the actions, scenes, or domains it shows, and prefer larger changes to the visual state for robustness. Our work establishes visual transition reasoning as a reusable foundation for systematic visual world-model training in MLLMs.
paper.title: WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs

figures.caption: RoboRSI framework. Given a task, the Manager organizes its skill hierarchy, the Planner composes an execution plan, and the Engineer runs the required skills. The Reviewer diagnoses failures from observations and tool traces, returning them for TSR-guided revision. Tested updates enter the next iteration, and stable branches become parameterized skills for subsequent tasks.

paper.abstract: A generalist robot should not only perform diverse tasks but also improve through experience, turning what it learns during execution into capabilities that later tasks can reuse. Robot agents that act through code can already repair programs from execution feedback, yet it remains a central challenge to organize this experience around the task structure that gives it meaning, so that each repair is attributed to the responsible capability, supported by execution evidence, and validated before it is reused. We introduce RoboRSI, a robot self-improvement system built on Top-Down Skill Refinement (TSR). TSR decomposes tasks into compound, atomic, and base skills with scoped responsibilities and explicit input--output contracts, attributes each execution outcome to the responsible branch, and confines revision to that branch. Building upon this structure, a Manager, Planner, Engineer, and Reviewer coordinate planning, execution, diagnosis, and the validated release of new skills, while people steer the process through objectives and corrections; stable skill sequences are further consolidated into reusable compound skills. On a mobile manipulator, RoboRSI develops multi-object household cleanup over 104 rounds. In simulation, it achieves the highest success rate on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.7 to 11.0 percentage points.
paper.title: RoboRSI: Stable, efficient, and reusable robot self-evolution in complex real-world environments

Both models provide generic electrical explanations that could be inferred from the sparks alone, but fail to identify the brief sequence of separator removal and subsequent contact that triggers the discharge. paper.abstract: Streaming Video Large Language Models (VLMs) enable continuous video understanding, yet existing benchmarks focus on low-dynamic scenarios. Under bounded context budgets, models must balance temporal history, spatial resolution, and temporal granularity; sparse sampling at 1--2 FPS misses fast events. We introduce FastBench to evaluate high-dynamic perception in real-world video streams. Its trajectory-grounded pipeline combines QA generation from high-FPS clips, filtering of questions answerable at 2 FPS, answer verification using SAM3 and CoTracker3 trajectories, and three rounds of human inspection. FastBench contains 306 QA pairs across eight domains, six capabilities, and forward, instant, and backward temporal scopes, with human-annotated evidence intervals. We also present ProactiveFrame, a training-free baseline that adjusts incoming frame rates through text tokens. A dual-tier sliding window retains recent high-FPS observations while downsampling older ones into sparse history. Experiments reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model, Gemini-3.5-Flash, scores only 50.7%. Denser sampling improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 32.9% at 2 FPS to 44.6% at 24 FPS, but gains saturate as history is compressed. ProactiveFrame outperforms sparse uniform sampling by 5.4 and 1.5 percentage points, yet remains well below oracle-guided focusing, showing that current VLMs struggle to determine from the stream alone when finer temporal perception is needed. FastBench provides a testbed for high-dynamic streaming video understanding. Code and data: https://github.com/Ashone3/FastBench.
paper.title: FastBench: Can Streaming VLMs Perceive High-Dynamic Real-World Streams?

paper.abstract: Safe reinforcement learning commonly places safety and task performance in the same policy objective, where they can introduce competing updates. Safety filters separate them at action execution, but classical designs require an analytic safety function and dynamics model, and standard minimal-intervention filters are myopic to long-horizon task return because they minimize only instantaneous action deviation. Hard projections are also undefined when no safe action exists. We present FAITH, a feasibility-aware, model-free framework that approximates the optimal state-action safety value and amortizes minimal-intervention filtering with a feedforward network. The task policy optimizes the task return through the filtered dynamics, which recovers the feasible constrained problem without a competing safety term in the task-policy update. When no action satisfies the learned safety condition, the same filter approaches the action with minimum predicted peak harm. On a double integrator example and a Safety Gym environment, FAITH achieves the highest return among methods with no feasible-start violations and matches the lowest harm from infeasible starts. On a 29-DoF humanoid, it reaches a 99.95% safety rate while retaining 97% of the unfiltered return in Walking-Avoid, and obtains the highest measured safety rate in Push-Avoid by learning to sacrifice balancing and fall away from the protected region. The same policies are also demonstrated on a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid.
paper.title: FAITH: Feasibility-Aware Safety-Filtered RL for High-Dimensional Systems

paper.abstract: Teaching a humanoid to follow instructions with its whole body runs into two obstacles. Its action space is large and tightly coupled: legs, arms, and fingers must move together while the robot keeps its balance, which makes joint-level actions hard to learn. And humanoid demonstrations are scarce, so current humanoid generalist policies do not follow new instructions out of the box and are fine-tuned on teleoperated demonstrations of each task before deployment. Human demonstrations exist in far larger numbers, but a person's motion is not a robot command. We remove both obstacles by changing what the generalist policy predicts. We introduce VioLA, a generalist humanoid policy that predicts body and hand motion latents instead of joint commands. A pretrained body- and hand-controller execute these latents on the robot. Their corresponding motion encoders map human and robot motion into the same latent spaces. A human recording is therefore labeled in the policy's action space, and the training demonstration pool contains 140.6 million frames, 93.2% of them human. As a result, VioLA follows locomotion instructions on the real robot zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, reaching 100% success where GR00T N1.7 and $\Psi_0$ reach 16.7% and 0%, respectively. It also reaches 88.6% manipulation success without task-specific fine-tuning. The same approach works across two VLA and one world-action model backbones. A generalist policy trained on human demonstrations alone performs locomotion tasks on the real robot zero-shot. Code and checkpoints will be released.
paper.title: VioLA: Learning Generalist Humanoid Control Policies from Human Data

paper.abstract: Human demonstrations are a scalable data source for learning dexterous manipulation, but the embodiment gap prevents human motion from being executed directly on robots. Inverse kinematics (IK) retargets human motion to robots efficiently but ignores dynamics, often producing infeasible motions. Reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) are commonly employed to yield dynamically feasible motions, but both are sample-inefficient and sensitive to hyperparameters. RL suffers from costly and unstable training and tedious reward engineering; MPC avoids policy optimization, yet retargets each trajectory in isolation, and solving one does not make the next easier. Sampling cost grows rapidly with dataset size and task difficulty. We hypothesize that dynamically feasible trajectories concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold shared across demonstrations, so that retargeting can be reduced to sampling from that manifold, conditioned on human motion, rather than solving a fresh optimization problem for every demonstration. We propose \textbf{Generative Neural Retargeting} (GNR), which uses a flow matching model to sample feasible trajectories. GNR outperforms MPC with only $8.5\%$ of the samples required by MPC, achieving a success rate of $56.20\%$ compared to $27.20\%$ for MPC. GNR can be used for scalable and efficient retargeting of large-scale, long-horizon, and millimeter precision human demonstrations: by applying GNR within a real-to-sim data engine, we produce a dexterous manipulation dataset with dense contact-force labels, spanning $223$k demonstrations and $3.3$k object geometries.
paper.title: Generative Neural Retargeting for Human-to-Robot Dexterous Manipulation

paper.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful foundations for robotic manipulation, but their reliance on fixed camera configurations during training makes them brittle to changes in camera count or pose during deployment. To overcome these limitations, we propose VersaCamVLA, a camera-configurable framework that decouples camera-set representation from action learning. VersaCamVLA learns a unified scene-token interface that maps an arbitrary, variable set of posed RGB views into fixed-size latent scene tokens. This is achieved via multi-signal target-view prediction and Wrist-Augmented Pose Sampling (WAPS), which leverages natural wrist-camera motion for free pose diversity. At deployment, a lightweight spatial encoder injects these compact scene tokens into a pretrained base VLA as a supplementary visual condition, requiring no explicit 3D sensing or novel-view rendering. Experiments on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real-robot platform demonstrate that VersaCamVLA consistently outperforms prior VLA methods and direct multi-view baselines, maintaining robust performance across varying camera counts and unseen camera poses.
paper.title: VersaCamVLA: Camera-Configurable VLA Policies for Robotic Manipulation

analysis.analysis: 作者将精细操作失败归因于空间可观测性不足而非策略能力不足，并通过在测试时提供虚拟互补视图来检验这一假设，即在保持冻结策略条件下改善任务关键空间关系的呈现。

evidence.claim: 作者认为精细操作失败的重要原因是空间可观测性不足，而非策略能力不足。

evidence.quote: We introduce SpatialHarness, a test-time embodied harness that provides test-time spatial scaffolding for fine robotic manipulation without policy fine-tuning or changes to the physical sensing setup.

evidence.claim: SpatialHarness 维护与真实执行同步的在线仿真场景，识别任务关键空间关系，并渲染互补虚拟视图给冻结的多模态策略。
evidence.quote: SpatialHarness maintains an online simulated scene synchronized with real-world execution, identifies task-critical spatial relationships, and renders complementary virtual views that expose them to a frozen multimodal policy.

evidence.claim: 为保持仿真场景对齐，作者开发了区分静态、被持和过渡模式的交互感知场景同步。

(b) Stationary object poses are retained or visually aligned according to movability. For continuously grasped objects, poses are predicted through physics simulation and validated; rejected predictions are replaced with visual estimates. When a grasp is established or released, the same measured motion segment is replayed from candidate pre-interaction poses to select the current state by interaction consistency and visual matching. paper.abstract: Frontier multimodal foundation models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra) have recently shown strong potential for direct robotic control, yet their performance on fine manipulation remains limited. We argue that an important source of failure is not necessarily insufficient policy capability, but insufficient spatial observability, where task-critical spatial relationships may be poorly revealed by the existing physical camera setup. We introduce SpatialHarness, a test-time embodied harness that provides test-time spatial scaffolding for fine robotic manipulation without policy fine-tuning or changes to the physical sensing setup. SpatialHarness maintains an online simulated scene synchronized with real-world execution, identifies task-critical spatial relationships, and renders complementary virtual views that expose them to a frozen multimodal policy. To keep the simulated scene aligned during interaction, we develop interaction-aware scene synchronization that distinguishes static, held, and transition modes. We evaluate SpatialHarness on four real-robot manipulation tasks spanning precise geometric alignment, object-relative placement, and articulated-object interaction. Using the same frozen GPT-6 Astra policy, SpatialHarness substantially improves task success, including from 26.7% to 66.7% on plug insertion and from 0% to 100% on Tower of Hanoi. These results indicate that improving spatial observability at test time can unlock fine-manipulation capabilities already present in strong multimodal foundation models. Project website: https://emilia113.github.io/SpatialHarness/.
paper.title: SpatialHarness: Test-Time Spatial Scaffolding for Fine Robotic Manipulation

analysis.analysis: 作者通过区分开放环生成、依赖冻结执行器的闭环系统与间接验证系统，指出规划动作和成功执行之间存在差距，并据此提出将程序化视频生成形式化为视觉世界空间中的闭环任务执行。材料未说明更具体的定量分析过程。
challenges: 长时序程序化任务需要根据已生成状态选择下一步动作并识别任务完成
开放环生成无法适应执行结果
现有闭环系统依赖预训练执行器或间接验证，规划动作可能无法被执行器实现
缺乏用于联合训练规划器和执行器的逐步动作-视频监督数据
长时序执行中需要维护状态并控制历史 token 成本

evidence.claim: 作者将程序化视频生成形式化为视觉世界空间中的闭环任务执行。
evidence.quote: We formulate procedural video generation as \emph{closed-loop task execution in visual world space} and introduce \textbf{WorldGuide}.

evidence.claim: WorldGuide 根据初始图像和任务目标预测原子动作、生成视频片段，并用生成结果选择下一步或终止。
evidence.quote: Given only an initial image and a task goal, WorldGuide predicts an atomic action, generates its corresponding video clip, and uses the generated result to select the next action or terminate.

evidence.claim: Planner 和 Executor 在同一套步骤级程序化演示上训练。
evidence.quote: The Planner and Executor are trained on the same step-level procedural demonstrations: the Planner learns to predict the next atomic action or task completion from visual progress, while the Executor is directly trained to realize the predicted actions.

evidence.claim: 分层视觉记忆在长时序执行中维护状态并限制历史 token 成本。
evidence.quote: Hierarchical visual memory maintains state across long-horizon execution with bounded history token cost.

evidence.claim: 作者构建了 WorldGuide Bench，包含约 59K 步骤标注视频、245 个任务和 27 个程序化类别。
evidence.quote: we introduce \textbf{WorldGuide Bench}: approximately 59K step-annotated videos across 245 tasks and 27 procedural categories.

evidence.claim: WorldGuide 在 WorldGuide-Bench 上取得 33.33% Task Success，高于 MiniMax-H3 的 29.90%。
evidence.quote: WorldGuide achieves a 33.33\% Task Success on \textbf{WorldGuide-Bench}, compared with 29.90\% for the strong recent video model MiniMax-H3

evidence.claim: WorldGuide 在 VideoCraft-Bench 的仅目标条件下取得 47.69%，对比 MiniMax-H3 的 32.73%。
evidence.quote: achieves 47.69\% on \textbf{VideoCraft-Bench} compared with 32.73\% for MiniMax-H3 under goal-only conditioning.

evidence.claim: 现有闭环系统常依赖预训练执行器或间接验证，导致决策动作与成功实现之间存在差距。
evidence.quote: Open-loop generation cannot adapt to execution outcomes, while existing closed-loop systems often rely on pretrained executors or indirect verification. This leaves a gap between deciding an action and successfully realizing it.

experiments: 在 WorldGuide-Bench 上，WorldGuide 达到 33.33% Task Success，而近期强视频模型 MiniMax-H3 为 29.90%，即使 MiniMax-H3 接收了参考动作计划。
在 VideoCraft-Bench 上，WorldGuide 在仅目标条件下达到 47.69%，而 MiniMax-H3 为 32.73%。
作者还在 WorldGuide Bench 上报告其方法取得最高的 Aesthetic Quality 和 Overall Consistency。
WorldGuide Bench 包含约 59K 步骤标注视频，覆盖 245 个任务和 27 个程序化类别，测试集使用 980 个视频。
analysis.first_affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
analysis.insight: 程序化视频生成应被建模为视觉世界空间中的闭环任务执行；下一步动作和任务终止应基于已经实际生成的视觉状态来决定，规划与执行必须共享同一套逐步程序化演示监督。
limitations: 仍存在差距，长时序执行需要更鲁棒的方法。
失败通常源于 Planner 过早或冗余的动作，或 Executor 生成的片段没有完全实现预期的状态转换。
由于每个生成状态会馈入下一次决策，这类错误可能传播。
作者提出未来可通过更丰富的状态有效性信号和显式恢复来加强耦合。
Executor 已基于 ContextPlanner 的动作嵌入进行条件生成，联合优化两个模块是自然的下一步。
有界视觉记忆会压缩旧状态以控制推理成本，更选择性保留任务相关信息可望改善长时序一致性并保持效率。
method: 给定初始图像和任务目标，WorldGuide 预测一个原子动作，生成对应视频片段，并使用生成结果选择下一个动作或终止。
Planner 和 Executor 在同一套步骤级程序化演示上训练。
Planner 从视觉进展中学习预测下一个原子动作或任务完成。
Executor 被直接训练以实现预测的动作。
采用分层视觉记忆在长时序执行中维护状态，并限制历史 token 成本。
构建 WorldGuide Bench 数据集，提供步骤级动作-视频监督以支持联合训练。
analysis.motivation: 开放环生成无法根据执行结果进行调整，而现有闭环系统往往依赖预训练执行器或间接验证，导致正确规划的动作仍可能无法被可靠执行，因此需要将规划与执行耦合，使规划基于不断演变的视觉状态，并让执行器直接学习实现预测动作。
analysis.primary_topic: 目标导向的视频世界模型，用于程序化任务的闭环执行
analysis.relation_to_research: 该工作直接关联具身智能、世界模型和物理人工智能：它研究视觉世界空间中的闭环任务执行，涉及可执行动作生成、长时序预测、规划与执行耦合、视觉记忆和推理效率，并可在程序化任务评测中体现真实任务完成能力。与视觉语言动作模型和世界动作模型相比，它侧重视觉世界模型中的动作选择与执行闭环，而非机器人底层控制。
analysis.setting: 给定初始图像和任务目标，模型需要逐步预测原子动作、生成对应视频片段，并利用生成结果选择下一步动作或终止任务，从而实现视觉世界空间中的闭环程序化任务执行。

analysis.uncertainty: 证据范围仅为摘要和全文节选，未提供完整的实验细节、评价协议、消融和研究限制外的更多数值；因此对方法细节、实验公平性和泛化能力的判断存在不确定性。
analysis.why_recommended: 值得当前研究者阅读，因为它将视频生成从开放环合成推进到闭环任务执行，提出规划器-执行器联合训练、分层视觉记忆和步骤级监督数据集，并给出与强视频模型的阶段性对比结果，对可执行动作生成、长时序预测、推理效率和真实任务评测均有直接参考价值。

figures.caption: From open-loop synthesis to learned procedural execution. (a) Open-loop generation follows a fixed prompt with no intermediate decisions, so it can drift into a wrong step and keep generating after the task is done. (b) A planner can inspect outcomes and replan, but with a frozen pretrained executor, a correct instruction can still fail to execute. (c) WorldGuide trains the ContextPlanner and Executor on the same demonstrations, the Executor conditioned on the planner’s action embeddings. Thus, generated outcomes guide the next action and the decision to stop.

Given the initial image x 0 x_{0} , task goal g g , and the latest K = 3 K{=}3 clip–action pairs h t h_{t} , the ContextPlanner π θ \pi_{\theta} predicts the next atomic action a t a_{t} or 𝙳𝙾𝙽𝙴 \mathtt{DONE} . The Executor f ϕ f_{\phi} renders a t a_{t} into the next clip x t + 1 x_{t+1} from the current visual state x t x_{t} and hierarchical memory M t M_{t} , which progressively compresses older latent frames. Each new clip x t + 1 x_{t+1} becomes the next visual state, is paired with a t a_{t} in the history h t + 1 h_{t+1} , and updates the memory M t + 1 M_{t+1} , and the loop continues until 𝙳𝙾𝙽𝙴 \mathtt{DONE} is predicted or the step budget is reached. paper.abstract: Video generators and video-based world models can synthesize plausible visual trajectories, but long-horizon procedural tasks require generation to adapt to what has actually been produced. A model must determine the next action from its generated state, execute that action, and recognize when the task is complete. Open-loop generation cannot adapt to execution outcomes, while existing closed-loop systems often rely on pretrained executors or indirect verification. This leaves a gap between deciding an action and successfully realizing it. We formulate procedural video generation as \emph{closed-loop task execution in visual world space} and introduce \textbf{WorldGuide}. Given only an initial image and a task goal, WorldGuide predicts an atomic action, generates its corresponding video clip, and uses the generated result to select the next action or terminate. The Planner and Executor are trained on the same step-level procedural demonstrations: the Planner learns to predict the next atomic action or task completion from visual progress, while the Executor is directly trained to realize the predicted actions. Hierarchical visual memory maintains state across long-horizon execution with bounded history token cost. Due to the lack of step-level action-video supervision for joint planner-executor training, we introduce \textbf{WorldGuide Bench}: approximately 59K step-annotated videos across 245 tasks and 27 procedural categories. WorldGuide achieves a 33.33\% Task Success on \textbf{WorldGuide-Bench}, compared with 29.90\% for the strong recent video model MiniMax-H3, even though MiniMax-H3 receives reference action plans, and achieves 47.69\% on \textbf{VideoCraft-Bench} compared with 32.73\% for MiniMax-H3 under goal-only conditioning. These results demonstrate the importance of coupling planning with learned execution for goal-directed procedural video generation.
paper.title: WorldGuide: Goal-Directed Video World Model for Procedural Task Execution

paper.abstract: General-purpose robots must perform a wide range of tasks from agile locomotion to dexterous manipulation. While sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has proven to be a useful tool for this goal, current RL pipelines depend on engineering-heavy, per-task structural priors such as shaped rewards and demonstrations. Recent work has shown that diverse simulator resets, combined with massively parallel simulation, can alleviate much of this engineering burden on several manipulation problems. However, we find that naively scaling this paradigm to more precise or dynamic problems remains non-trivial. While simulator resets can help with exploration, uniformly sampling over this distribution wastes a growing fraction of learning experience on task configurations the policy has already mastered or cannot yet attempt. This makes it challenging to see the expected benefits of scaling parallel environments for RL, since much of the learning signal in a batch is wasted during learning. To mitigate this, we introduce Success Guided Sampling (SGS), a simple adaptive sampler that concentrates RL training on task configurations around the frontier of the policy's capabilities. Doing so allows large-scale simulated RL to make the most out of the experience in a batch, enabling much more effective scaling to large-scale parallel simulation. Across experiments using up to $2^{20}$ (over one million) parallel environments, SGS enables RL to solve challenging multi-terrain quadruped locomotion and contact-rich assembly tasks that prior methods fail to solve. Finally, we distill the learned manipulation policies into RGB-based policies and demonstrate zero-shot transfer to several challenging assembly tasks on real hardware. Project website: https://sgs-rl.github.io/.
paper.title: A Balanced Data Diet: Addressing the Exploration Bottleneck in Mega-Scale RL for Robot Control

paper.abstract: We present DreamTrue, a multi-view, cross-embodiment robot world model for action-faithful and physically plausible video prediction. Training such a model on existing robot datasets faces two obstacles: imprecise calibration can impair action following, while limited coverage of unsuccessful interactions can bias predictions toward successful outcomes. To improve action following across embodiments, we render action trajectories into image-space conditions and introduce offline geometric calibration to align these conditions with the target videos. To broaden interaction coverage, we introduce counterfactual post-training, modifying recorded action trajectories and generating future videos under a wider range of actions and contact configurations. To provide feedback on these predictions without paired ground-truth futures, we construct a human-annotated video dataset covering robot, object, and interaction defects and use it to train an embodied video reward model. Its scores guide reinforcement-learning post-training toward more physically plausible interaction outcomes. On AgiBot, DreamTrue attains state-of-the-art action following, while reducing the human-assessed interaction defect rate from from 48.12% to 6.25%. Notably, our model ranks first in the world model track of the AgiBot World Challenge 2026. The project page can be found at https://brave-eai.github.io/DreamTrue.
paper.title: DreamTrue: Action-Faithful Robot World Model with Counterfactual Post-Training

figures.caption: Overview of Dex-One2Many. (1) From a single human video, a VLM extracts a stage-wise scene graph of object relations. (2) Each stage graph constrains the sampling of object poses and synthesized grasps, yielding verified reset states for every stage. An RL policy trained from these resets with predicate-derived rewards acts in task space through a QP controller. (3) The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen initial poses, goal poses, and grasps on real hardware.
figures.label: Figure 2

paper.abstract: While learning dexterous manipulation from a single human video offers a promising alternative to costly robot demonstrations, many recent methods predominantly imitate demonstrated motions. Such strict motion matching often limits generalization to initial object poses, goal poses, and grasps not shown in the video. Alternatively, discovering a policy via reinforcement learning (RL) allows for broad generalization, but without prior guidance, it struggles with high-dimensional exploration in complex, multi-stage tasks. To address these coupled generalization and exploration challenges, we present Dex-One2Many, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that learns a generalizable dexterous manipulation policy from a single human video. Our key insight is to abstract the video into sequential scene graphs that guide RL, enabling efficient exploration while preserving broad generalizability. The graphs serve as generative constraints for sampling diverse reset states and provide dense rewards for each stage. Because the graphs constrain relations rather than exact poses, these reset states cover object poses and grasps beyond the video, while initializing each stage from them with dense rewards keeps exploration short and guided. Trained entirely in simulation, Dex-One2Many transfers zero-shot to a real multi-fingered hand. Across five tool-use and manipulation tasks, Dex-One2Many exceeds baselines by 6.5% in seen configurations, while its robust generalization widens this gap to 71% in unseen scenarios.
paper.title: Dex-One2Many: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from a Single Human Demonstration

paper.abstract: Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena, presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic evaluation under these conditions, we introduce DexBioLab, a simulation benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments. DexBioLab comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large-scale data generation and evaluation, we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay for demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop policy evaluation. Our evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://cumulusalpha.github.io/DexBioLabWebPage.
paper.title: DexBioLab: Benchmarking Dexterous Manipulation with Dynamic Experimental Phenomena in Realistic Laboratories

figures.caption: Overview of the HorizonNav framework. Visual reasoning and exploration planning: a VLM analyzes the initial RGB image and language task to generate structured exploration commands. Exploratory video generation: Wan 2.2 synthesizes plausible future observations along multiple virtual camera trajectories. Geometry-guided 3D reconstruction: ORB-SLAM3 estimates camera poses and sparse landmarks, while Video Depth Anything predicts dense depth maps. Landmark-guided depth alignment, multi-view registration, and point-cloud fusion produce a geometrically consistent imagined 3D map for subsequent robot navigation and path planning.
figures.label: Figure 1

figures.caption: Qualitative generated-view geometry. Left: representative exploration branches showing generated RGB, dense-depth diagnostic, ORB-SLAM3 sparse structure, and corresponding real-view references. Right: reconstructed structure registered to the external LiDAR reference for visualization and evaluation; LiDAR is not available to HorizonNav during reconstruction or planning.
figures.label: Figure 2

paper.abstract: We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar. Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
paper.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
paper.title: HorizonNav: Geometry-Guided Video Diffusion for Anticipatory 3D Robot Navigation

figures.caption: Overview of the standard LapMerge pipeline. Given an ordered sequence of M M input tokens, LapMerge produces exactly N N budget-exact, soft-merged output tokens. A learned scorer assigns each input token a mass, represented as a Laplace kernel. The summed density is scanned cumulatively and partitioned into N N equal-mass segments, each of which is collapsed into a single output token. The resulting N N tokens are then processed by a Transformer classifier. The rightmost panel shows a real histopathology slide with the learned scorer weights overlaid on the tissue; opacity indicates the importance attributed to each patch. These same scores determine the token merging and can therefore be read as a learned routing-mass map: a direct view of where the model allocates its token budget.
figures.label: Figure 1

paper.abstract: Modern vision and language models process ever longer token sequences, and reducing them is the main lever on downstream cost. Token compression, however, faces a fundamental trade-off: selecting tokens discards information, while existing merging methods preserve it only through pairwise token-to-token matching or $MN$ token-to-output interactions. We introduce LapMerge, a differentiable merging operator that resolves this trade-off for ordered sequences: a learned mass distribution partitions the sequence into exactly $N$ equal-mass segments under a Laplace-kernel density, and prefix/suffix scans aggregate each segment, so both the forward and the backward pass run in $\mathcal{O}(M+N)$ time. This combination - an exact output budget, end-to-end differentiability, and linear cost - is precisely what previous reducers trade off against one another. The budget can be changed without changing operator parameters, and the learned mass doubles as a token-level map of where the budget is allocated. Across vision and vision-language tasks, LapMerge matches or improves on strong token reducers while being up to two orders of magnitude faster at large sequence lengths; it is particularly effective when token order reflects spatial or temporal locality, and works both as a drop-in reduction module and as a trainable architectural component.
paper.title: LapMerge: Differentiable Exact-Budget Token Merging in Linear Time

paper.abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. We propose BT-Agent, an onboard architecture combining LLM-driven task decisions with predefined behavior-tree (BT) skills. These skills enforce execution conditions and return structured failure feedback. We demonstrate fully onboard operation with a 9B model on a quadruped across five task categories. Intervention tests show that local checks stop ongoing navigation without waiting for another model decision, while the agent remains active to retry or report constraints. To compare agent designs efficiently, we introduce a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark, evaluated in text on all tasks and in Habitat on 39. Text supports 10.9$\times$ higher evaluation throughput, while simulation reveals how perception and motion failures change task outcomes. BT-Agent's largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.
paper.title: BT-Agent: Deploying Onboard Robot Agents with Behavior Trees and Multi-Fidelity Evaluation

analysis.uncertainty: 仅有标题与摘要，无法确认具体模型架构、数据集规模、数值结果、显著性水平、EICS 与 CASP-VL 的详细定义及作者陈述的局限；相关工作与实验细节均未知。

paper.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly analyze and reason about images, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations faithfully encode the structured relations required for such reasoning. We introduce EICS (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for testing whether representations consistently encode concepts under controlled one-concept interventions, and CASP-VL (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, we find that spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information, even when the same models score well above chance on compositional benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation, whether through the (EOS) token or by mean pooling. These findings reveal a systematic failure invisible to output-based evaluation: VLMs do not preserve, in the representation used downstream, relational information that is present in their own input.
paper.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors

analysis.analysis: 摘要与全文节选表明，作者通过条件世界模型适配触发机制、组件与兼容性检查以及递归保留协议来分析问题；但材料未说明部分分析细节，如具体误差、校准、漂移和覆盖判据的完整定义。

experiments: 代码修复中，编码器固定，使用 200 个 CodeContests 任务、三个随机种子、最多三轮反馈，在线测试提供反馈，隐藏测试衡量最终成功率。

经过世界模型适配后成功率进一步提升至 31.2%；相对静态验证器的配对增益为 +2.83 个百分点（95% 区间 [+0.17, +5.50]）。

经过五个连续策略版本，实验室规划得分从 21.80% 提升至 46.01%，实现翻倍以上增长。
在相同 40 次实验预算下，反应优化中 RSI-Anything 达到 96.15% 的平均最佳观测产率，而贝叶斯优化为 82.16%。

paper.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.
paper.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models

figures.caption: Timing-related issues in robot policy learning. (a) Real robot systems exhibit multiple sources of temporal variation, including variable sensor sampling rate, observation latency and dropout, inference latency, control frequency, and execution latency. These timing effects matter differently across tasks. (b) In dynamic tasks, the key temporal relationship is between when an observation is captured and when an action takes effect . (c) In multisensory tasks, the key temporal relationship is between when different observations are captured . (d) Even in quasi-static tasks, differences between data-collection and deployment timing can create temporal mismatch. Standard fixed-rate policy representations obscure these distinctions by treating sequence position as a proxy for time.
figures.label: Figure 1

figures.caption: Overview of Chronos Policy. Tokens are paired with their physical times. Time-aware RoPE uses these physical timestamps as positional coordinates, so attention depends on elapsed time rather than sequence index. The diffusion transformer then predicts an action chunk at the requested execution times.
figures.label: Figure 2

paper.abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation-action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy, which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.
paper.title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time

However, its noise distribution can deviate from standard Gaussian, with associated unsafe motions and emergency-stop interventions on real robots. In contrast, NSL-AWR is better suited to interaction-limited real-robot adaptation, combining lower computational cost with safer execution.

experiments: 在 LIBERO-10 上使用 SmolVLA 与 π0.5 的 Full 与 One demonstration 设定评估；所有三种 NSL 方法均超过基础策略参考。
Full 设定下峰值成功率：SmolVLA 达 95.8%，π0.5 达 99.8%；One 设定下分别从 24.4% 和 40.4% 提升至 77.0% 和 71.2%。
NSL-PPO 在两种 Full 设定下接近 NSL-SAC，并在两种 One 设定下超过 NSL-AWR 的峰值。
真实机器人任务：杯子堆叠、玩具钓鱼、顺序插入、珠子放置，使用经监督微调初始化的任务特定 π0.5 策略。
真实机器人比较：NSL-AWR 与 Action-AWR、RLT 对比；有人的引导时 NSL-AWR 与 DAgger、UniSteer 对比；每任务评估 40 次试验。
真实机器人结果：NSL-AWR 在人引导下耗时 2.04 分钟；相比 Action-AWR 与 RLT 的训练时间（摘要节选中显示 23.2 分钟对应 RLT）更少，且在每个任务上每轮使用的人类轨迹少于 UniSteer 同时平均成功率更高。
模拟中 NSL-SAC 在交互预算充足时表现最佳但计算需求更高，且噪声分布可能偏离标准高斯，在真实机器人上伴随不安全动作与急停；NSL-AWR 更适合交互受限的真实机器人适配，计算成本更低且执行更安全。

paper.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. Building on prior noise-steering methods, we formulate NSL as an interface for VLA adaptation that accommodates different learning algorithms and instantiate it with PPO, SAC, and AWR. Theoretically, we provide an information-theoretic analysis of how NSL enables efficient adaptation. Empirically, we study these NSL algorithms on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks under interaction, computation, and execution constraints. Across these settings, we develop a suite of effective NSL variants and derive practical recommendations for choosing among them under different resource and deployment regimes.
paper.title: Noise Space Learning for VLA Adaptation

paper.abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific scene and object set using only a handheld phone scan and images of the user's objects. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m$^2$ and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. These results suggest that automated real-to-sim-to-real training can personalize VLA manipulation policies using only simulation-oracle data.
paper.title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation

paper.abstract: In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.
paper.title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark

paper.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, yet most existing methods make decisions primarily from the current observation. This limits their reliability in long-horizon tasks, where visually similar states may correspond to different interaction histories and task stages. Moreover, directly incorporating historical observations can introduce stale, stage-mismatched, or error-contaminated information, leading to inaccurate world prediction and accumulated closed-loop errors. We propose RM-WAM, a reliable memory-augmented World Action Model that treats memory as a context-dependent predictive resource rather than universally useful historical context. RM-WAM represents history using complementary short-term visual state memory and latent event memory, which respectively capture recent interaction dynamics and longer-term state transitions. A counterfactual memory learning scheme varies the accessible history while keeping the current inputs and prediction targets fixed, enabling the model to learn a context-dependent utility estimate for historical memory. Based on this estimate, a utility-aware gating mechanism adaptively controls memory injection into the world-action backbone. Experiments demonstrate that RM-WAM highlights the importance of reliable and selective memory utilization in long-horizon tasks.
paper.title: RM-WAM: Reliable Memory-Augmented World Action Models for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation

paper.abstract: Visual self-modelling lets robots learn body models from observations, but such models usually encode kinematics implicitly rather than exposing metric joint parameters for computation and control. Moreover, a good fit to images does not by itself establish accurate kinematics. Here we present an explicit analytic robot self-model that requires neither deformation networks nor URDF/CAD templates. Multi-view images and joint readings establish Gaussian appearance and provide motion evidence for rigid link assignments, whereas sparse end-effector poses independently identify metric screw axes. The resulting closed-form forward kinematics and analytic Jacobian can be evaluated beyond the fitting ranges. We validate the model on a simulated seven-axis arm, a simulated twelve-joint quadruped and a real six-axis arm. In simulation, it achieves millimetre-level reaching and pick-and-place, as well as closed-loop quadruped walking. On the real arm, it renders held-out configurations, predicts end-effector positions with a median error of 6.4 mm, compared with 11.7 mm for a calibrated nominal model, and supports reaching with external marker feedback. A controlled comparison shows that image fit alone is not enough: two Panda models differing only in their joint axes are 0.55 dB apart in PSNR, yet their end-effector prediction errors differ 13.7-fold.
paper.title: Analytic Robot Self-Model: Learning Screw-Axis Kinematics for Rendering and Model-Based Control

paper.abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error. Videos and further details are available on the project website: https://rapwam.github.io/.
paper.title: RAP-WAM: Learning World-Action Models through Predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations

paper.abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

figures.caption: Overview of UniLAP. Stage I pretrains a continuous flow-matching latent action policy (LAP) on action-free videos under ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} . A frozen LAM teacher’s posterior is distilled via the flow-adaptive ℒ distill \mathcal{L}_{\text{distill}} , and a cross-frame correspondence target supervises the motion predictor to regularize the latent. Stage II attaches a per-embodiment decoder ϕ dec \phi_{\text{dec}} , trains it from scratch, and finetunes the latent policy on the target embodiment’s labeled actions.

paper.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
paper.title: UniLAP: A Unified Latent Action Policy for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation

figures.caption: TacitVLA retains the benefit of reasoning supervision without conditioning its actions on the generated text. Left: how the policies act in one call. Given the context c t c_{t} , on memory tasks including the ledger M t M_{t} of past subtasks, the backbone generates the reasoning r t r_{t} and conditions the action expert that outputs the action chunk a t a_{t} . In Explicit Reasoning , the action expert attends to r t r_{t} , so every action chunk waits for it. TacitVLA trains on the same sequence with r t r_{t} masked from the action expert, bypassing the need to generate r t r_{t} on non-memory tasks. On memory tasks, r t r_{t} still becomes the next ledger entry (dashed loop), but is generated asynchronously during execution instead of making the action expert wait. No Reasoning is the same architecture trained without reasoning supervision. Right: TacitVLA matches Explicit Reasoning’s success at 1.7 × \times and 3.4 × \times lower latency, and matches No Reasoning’s latency at +3.5% and +5.3% success (Tables 3 , 5 , 15 ).

paper.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
paper.title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency

WoVR+ extends WoVR’s reliability-oriented framework to complete VLA interfaces with multi-view observations and proprioceptive feedback, as well as long-horizon, multi-stage manipulation. paper.abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.
paper.title: WoVR+: World Model as Reliable Simulator for Versatile VLA Policy Optimization with RL

paper.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.
paper.title: WAVE-0: Bridging VLA Policies and WAMs with Lightweight Latent Future Prediction

paper.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.
paper.title: ForkCast: Predictive Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Policies via Counterfactual Futures

paper.abstract: World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

paper.title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models

evidence.quote: We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator.

paper.abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from $\pi_{0.5}$ and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
paper.title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics

paper.abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.
paper.title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning

paper.abstract: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/.
paper.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions

analysis.analysis: 作者通过视觉条件化的联合动作-触觉重建学习交互潜变量，并用时间条件隐式解码器实现；通过潜在响应对动作与触觉缩放的敏感性、对高斯噪声的响应，以及线性探针评估冻结交互编码器输出中保留的运动与接触信息（如力代理幅值 L1 从 3.548 降至 0.195，动作 L1 从 0.0676 升至 0.0837），分析表示对接触信息的保留能力。

evidence.claim: ILA 将运动、接触与力施加的联合演化表示为可解码的交互潜变量，作为策略动作单元
evidence.quote: We propose ILA (Interaction Latents as Actions), which uses decodable interaction latents that jointly capture the evolution of motion, contact, and force application as policy action units

evidence.claim: 多数策略主要把动作表示为运动轨迹，未在动作表示中显式编码接触动力学
evidence.quote: Yet most robot policies represent actions primarily as motion trajectories, using tactile signals as inputs or auxiliary prediction targets without explicitly encoding contact dynamics in the action representation.

evidence.claim: 交互潜变量支持预训练 VLA 与 WAM 的后训练，以及从头训练流匹配策略
evidence.quote: Using them as flow-matching generation targets supports post-training of pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs), as well as training flow-matching policies from scratch.

evidence.claim: 共享解码器将生成的潜变量映射为可执行动作
evidence.quote: A shared decoder maps generated latents to executable actions.

evidence.claim: ILA 在三个策略家族、四个真实任务上相对触觉条件化直接动作基线平均成功率提升 21.0-36.5 个百分点
evidence.quote: Across three policy families, ILA improves success rates averaged over four real-world tasks by 21.0-36.5 percentage points relative to tactile-conditioned direct-action baselines.

evidence.claim: 消融显示在动作目标中编码接触演化优于仅触觉条件化，且同一潜空间支持专家引导的离线改进
evidence.quote: Ablations highlight the benefit of encoding contact evolution in action targets beyond tactile conditioning, while the same latent space supports expert-guided offline improvement.

evidence.claim: 引入 ILA 的问题动机是运动轨迹本身不足以刻画相似运动的不同接触模式与不同运动-力组合

evidence.claim: 线性探针分析中 ILA 将力代理幅值 L1 从 3.548 降至 0.195，而动作 L1 从 0.0676 升至 0.0837

paper.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to coordinate not only where to move, but also how contact and force should evolve throughout an interaction. Yet most robot policies represent actions primarily as motion trajectories, using tactile signals as inputs or auxiliary prediction targets without explicitly encoding contact dynamics in the action representation. We propose ILA (Interaction Latents as Actions), which uses decodable interaction latents that jointly capture the evolution of motion, contact, and force application as policy action units, providing a shared representation for action generation, evaluation, and offline improvement. We learn these latents through visually conditioned joint action-tactile reconstruction with a time-conditioned implicit decoder. Using them as flow-matching generation targets supports post-training of pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs), as well as training flow-matching policies from scratch. A shared decoder maps generated latents to executable actions. For offline improvement, we learn a tactile-conditioned expert reference model from interaction latents encoded from expert demonstrations. The resulting expert-consistency rewards guide weighted learning from successful rollouts, while observation-compatible expert references guide correction of low-reward predictions from failed rollouts. Across three policy families, ILA improves success rates averaged over four real-world tasks by 21.0-36.5 percentage points relative to tactile-conditioned direct-action baselines. Ablations highlight the benefit of encoding contact evolution in action targets beyond tactile conditioning, while the same latent space supports expert-guided offline improvement. Project website: https://mrsecant.github.io/ILA/.
paper.title: Interaction Latents as Actions for Contact-Rich Manipulation

paper.abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. analysis.analysis: 作者观察到，子目标选定后原语序列由记忆规定，是常规性的，因此每个原语调用 LLM 推理是冗余的；LLM 计算应随决策数量而非原语数量扩展。
challenges: LLM 推理开销随原语数量线性增长，导致 episode 成本高昂
在保持泛化能力的同时减少 LLM 调用次数
将记忆编译为可自主执行的动作块并在失败时正确返回控制

evidence.claim: 智能体机器人中每个原语都需要一轮 LLM 推理，成本随原语数量增长。
evidence.quote: Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives.

evidence.claim: 作者发现子目标确定后的原语执行是冗余推理。
evidence.quote: We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory.

evidence.claim: 在线阶段单次调用启动链式原语块，仅在失败时返回控制。

paper.abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
paper.title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics

paper.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points, against -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy's reliance on the instruction unchanged.
paper.title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies

paper.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
paper.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
